title: Pandas for Data Handling
summary: Pandas is the go-to tool for loading, cleaning, and exploring tabular data. Before you train any model, you must understand and prepare your data. Pandas DataFrames give you a spreadsheet-like interface backed by NumPy speed, and data preparation typ
content:
# Pandas for Data Handling ##### Fourteen ways to write "Mumbai" A GenAI team in Nashik was building a retrieval chatbot over three years of customer support tickets. Before embedding anything, someone sensibly asked: which cities generate the most tickets? The answer would decide which regional language support they built first. The query returned 4,100 distinct city values for a country with a few hundred cities that mattered. `Mumbai`, `mumbai`, `MUMBAI`, `Mumbai `, ` Mumbai`, `Mumbai.`, `Bombay`, `Mumbai,MH`, `Mumbai - 400001`, `mumbai city`, `MUM`, `Greater Mumbai`, `Navi Mumbai`, and one entry that was just `M`. Fourteen spellings of one city, spread across 31,000 tickets. Their "Mumbai is 3% of tickets" number was wrong by a factor of five. They had nearly deprioritised Marathi support on the strength of it. There is an old figure that data scientists spend 80% of their time on data preparation. People quote it as a complaint. It is better understood as a description of where the value is: **the model can only be as good as what you feed it, and real data is always like this.** Pandas is the tool for finding and fixing it. ##### Series and DataFrames Pandas gives you two structures, both built on NumPy arrays from Day 3. A **Series** is a labelled 1-D array — one column. ```python import pandas as pd tickets_per_day = pd.Series([120, 145, 98, 210, 175], index=["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"], name="tickets") print(tickets_per_day["Thu"]) # 210 print(tickets_per_day.mean()) # 149.6 ``` A **DataFrame** is a table — a dict of Series sharing an index. ```python df = pd.DataFrame({ "ticket_id": ["T-001", "T-002", "T-003", "T-004"], "city": ["Mumbai", "mumbai ", "Pune", None], "category": ["billing", "technical", "billing", "technical"], "resolved": [True, False, True, True], "hours": [2.5, 14.0, 1.0, None], }) ``` The methods you run first, every single time, on any new dataset: ```python df.head(10) # first rows — eyeball the actual values df.shape # (rows, columns) df.info() # dtypes and non-null counts — the most useful single call df.describe() # summary stats for numeric columns df.dtypes df.columns.tolist() df["city"].value_counts(dropna=False) # THIS is how you find 14 Mumbais df.isna().sum() # missing count per column df.duplicated().sum() ``` `df.info()` and `value_counts(dropna=False)` are the two calls that would have caught the Nashik problem on day one. ##### Reading data ```python df = pd.read_csv("tickets.csv") # Real-world CSVs need arguments: df = pd.read_csv( "tickets.csv", parse_dates=["created_at"], # parse dates properly, not as strings dtype={"pincode": "string"}, # keep leading zeros — 400001 vs 011... na_values=["", "NA", "N/A", "null", "-", "unknown"], encoding="utf-8", thousands=",", # handle "1,20,000" ) # JSON — including the nested kind LLM APIs return records = pd.read_json("responses.json") flat = pd.json_normalize(nested_list, record_path="choices", meta=["id", "model"]) ``` Three arguments earn their keep constantly. **`parse_dates`** — otherwise dates are strings and `.dt` accessors will not work. **`dtype` for ID-like columns** — pincodes, phone numbers, and account IDs read as integers lose leading zeros and gain scientific notation. **`na_values`** — every dataset encodes missingness differently, and telling pandas up front converts a cleaning step into a parsing step. ##### Filtering and selection ```python # Single column -> Series; list of columns -> DataFrame city = df["city"] subset = df[["city", "category", "hours"]] # Boolean filtering — same idea as NumPy masking slow = df[df["hours"] > 8] billing_unresolved = df[(df["category"] == "billing") & (~df["resolved"])] # .isin() beats chained ORs metros = df[df["city"].isin(["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Bengaluru", "Chennai"])] # .query() reads nicely for complex conditions slow_billing = df.query("hours > 8 and category == 'billing'") ``` **Use `&`, `|`, `~` — not `and`, `or`, `not`** — and parenthesise each condition. This is the same rule as NumPy, for the same reason. **`.loc` and `.iloc`** are the explicit accessors, and you should prefer them: ```python df.loc[df["city"] == "Pune", "priority"] = "high" # label-based, and assignable df.iloc[0:5, 0:3] # position-based ``` `.loc` for filtering-and-assigning in one step is the correct way to modify a subset. Chained indexing (`df[df.city == "Pune"]["priority"] = "high"`) triggers the famous `SettingWithCopyWarning` and often silently does nothing. ##### Handling missing data First, understand the missingness. Then decide. ```python print(df.isna().sum()) print(df.isna().mean().round(3)) # fraction missing per column # Is missingness itself informative? print(df.groupby(df["hours"].isna())["resolved"].mean()) ``` That last line is worth internalising. If tickets with a missing `hours` value are resolved 12% of the time versus 84% otherwise, the missingness is not random — it probably means "never actually worked on." Dropping those rows would delete your most interesting cases. Your options: ```python df.dropna(subset=["ticket_id"]) # drop rows missing a key field df.dropna(axis=1, thresh=int(0.5 * len(df))) # drop columns >50% empty df["hours"] = df["hours"].fillna(df["hours"].median()) # median: outlier-robust df["city"] = df["city"].fillna("unknown") # explicit category df["priority"] = df["priority"].ffill() # carry last value forward df["hours_was_missing"] = df["hours"].isna().astype(int) # keep the signal ``` The last line is the most underrated: **add an indicator column before you impute**, so a downstream model can learn from the fact of missingness. Use the median rather than the mean for skewed numeric data — one ticket that took 900 hours will drag a mean imputation badly wrong. ##### The cleaning pipeline Here is the Nashik fix, written as reusable code: ```python import pandas as pd import re CITY_CANON = { "bombay": "Mumbai", "mum": "Mumbai", "greater mumbai": "Mumbai", "mumbai city": "Mumbai", "bangalore": "Bengaluru", "blr": "Bengaluru", "calcutta": "Kolkata", "madras": "Chennai", "poona": "Pune", "gurgaon": "Gurugram", } def standardise_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame: df = df.copy() df.columns = ( df.columns.str.strip().str.lower() .str.replace(r"[^\w]+", "_", regex=True).str.strip("_") ) return df def clean_city(df: pd.DataFrame, col: str = "city") -> pd.DataFrame: df = df.copy() s = ( df[col].astype("string") .str.strip() .str.replace(r"[.,\-]+$", "", regex=True) # trailing punctuation .str.replace(r"\s*[-,]\s*\d{6}$", "", regex=True) # trailing pincode .str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True) .str.lower() ) s = s.replace(CITY_CANON) # alias -> canonical df[col] = s.str.title() return df def clean_tickets(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame: df = pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["created_at"], na_values=["", "NA", "-", "unknown", "null"]) df = standardise_columns(df) df = clean_city(df) df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["ticket_id"], keep="last") df["hours_was_missing"] = df["hours"].isna().astype(int) df["hours"] = df["hours"].fillna(df["hours"].median()) df["category"] = df["category"].str.lower().str.strip().astype("category") return df clean = clean_tickets("tickets.csv") print(f"{clean['city'].nunique()} distinct cities after cleaning") ``` 4,100 distinct cities became 312. The alias dictionary handles the renamed cities, the regex handles the formatting noise, and `.str.title()` handles the casing. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Raw CSV
4,100 'cities'"] --> B["Standardise
column names"] B --> C["Strip whitespace
& punctuation"] C --> D["Lowercase"] D --> E["Map aliases
Bombay → Mumbai"] E --> F["Title case"] F --> G["Drop duplicate
ticket_ids"] G --> H["Flag + impute
missing values"] H --> I["Clean DataFrame
312 cities"] ``` ##### GroupBy and aggregation GroupBy is **split → apply → combine**: split rows into groups, compute something per group, stack the results back into a table. ```python # One metric, one group clean.groupby("city")["hours"].mean() # Several metrics at once, with names you choose summary = ( clean.groupby("city") .agg( tickets=("ticket_id", "count"), avg_hours=("hours", "mean"), median_hours=("hours", "median"), resolution_rate=("resolved", "mean"), ) .sort_values("tickets", ascending=False) .round(2) ) print(summary.head(10)) # Multiple grouping keys by_city_cat = clean.groupby(["city", "category"], observed=True)["hours"].mean() # Cross-tab view pivot = clean.pivot_table(index="city", columns="category", values="hours", aggfunc="median", fill_value=0) ``` Two habits: **always include a count** alongside your averages, because a 40-hour mean over three tickets means nothing; and use **`.agg()` with named outputs** so your columns arrive with sensible names instead of a MultiIndex you then have to flatten. `transform` is the sibling worth knowing — it returns a result aligned to the original rows rather than one row per group: ```python clean["city_avg_hours"] = clean.groupby("city")["hours"].transform("mean") clean["vs_city_avg"] = clean["hours"] - clean["city_avg_hours"] ``` ##### Merging and joining ```python agents = pd.DataFrame({ "agent_id": ["A1", "A2", "A3"], "agent_name": ["Priya S", "Rahul K", "Meera J"], "team": ["north", "west", "south"], }) merged = clean.merge( agents, on="agent_id", how="left", # keep all tickets, add agent info where it matches validate="many_to_one", # loud error if agents has duplicate agent_ids indicator=True, # adds a _merge column showing match status ) print(merged["_merge"].value_counts()) ``` The join types: `inner` keeps only matches, `left` keeps all of the left table, `right` the mirror, and `outer` keeps everything. **`validate=` is the argument nobody teaches and everybody needs.** If `agents` accidentally contains `A2` twice, a plain merge silently doubles those ticket rows and your counts are wrong with no warning. `validate="many_to_one"` turns that into an exception. Combined with a shape check before and after, it eliminates the most insidious class of pandas bug: ```python before = len(clean) merged = clean.merge(agents, on="agent_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one") assert len(merged) == before, f"Merge changed row count: {before} -> {len(merged)}" ``` Use `pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True)` to stack tables with the same columns vertically. ##### Common mistakes - **Never running `value_counts()` on categorical columns** — the fourteen-Mumbais failure. - **Chained indexing assignment** (`df[mask]["col"] = x`) instead of `df.loc[mask, "col"] = x`. - **`and`/`or` instead of `&`/`|`** in filters, or missing parentheses. - **Dropping all rows with any missing value** without checking how much data that destroys. - **Merging without checking row counts before and after.** - **Mean imputation on skewed data** where median is correct. - **Leaving dates as strings**, then failing to sort or resample. - **Losing leading zeros** on pincodes and IDs read as integers. - **Averaging without counts**, so tiny groups look like real signals. - **`inplace=True`** — it is being deprecated, it does not save memory, and it makes chaining impossible. Reassign instead. - **Iterating rows with `iterrows()`.** It is slow and returns copies; use vectorized operations or `.apply()` if you truly must. ##### Hands-on: clean something messy Your practical task uses the Titanic dataset: load it, inspect it, handle the missing values, and compute survival rate grouped by class and gender. Before imputing `Age`, run `df.groupby(df["Age"].isna())["Survived"].mean()` and see whether missing age is itself predictive — it usually is, and that observation is worth more than the imputation. The final groupby is two lines and produces a genuinely striking table. The mini project is the pipeline: a messy CSV in, standardised column names, filled missing values, deduplicated rows, and a clean dataset plus a summary report out. Write it as functions, as in the `clean_tickets` example above, not as one long script — that structure is what makes a pipeline reusable when the next messy CSV arrives. Have the report print before/after row counts, distinct-value counts per key column, and the missing-value table, so the cleaning is auditable rather than magical. The assignment asks for five insights from a dataset of your choice using groupby, filtering, and merging, documented in a notebook. Pick something you actually care about — `data.gov.in` has real Indian datasets on rainfall, crop prices, and railway performance. For each insight, write the finding as a sentence with a number in it before you write the code. That habit, from Day 41's storytelling discipline, is what turns a notebook into an analysis. ##### Key takeaways - **Real data is always messier than you expect.** Run `df.info()`, `df.isna().sum()`, and `value_counts(dropna=False)` on every new dataset before drawing a single conclusion. - **Read data with intent**: `parse_dates`, `dtype` for ID columns, and `na_values` turn three cleaning steps into parsing arguments. - **Investigate missingness before imputing** — whether a value is missing is often itself a signal, so flag it in a new column and use the median for skewed data. - **GroupBy is split-apply-combine**; always report a count alongside every average, and use `.agg()` with named outputs. - **Merges silently corrupt data.** Use `validate=`, `indicator=True`, and assert your row count before and after.
practical_task_reference: Load a public CSV (e.g., Titanic), inspect it, handle missing values, and compute survival rate grouped by class and gender.
mini_project_reference: Build a data-cleaning pipeline that ingests a messy CSV, standardizes column names, fills missing values, removes duplicates, and outputs a clean dataset with a summary report.
assignment_reference: Analyze a dataset of your choice: produce 5 insights using groupby, filtering, and merging, documented in a Jupyter notebook.
